name: Copernicus's deathbed book
scope: The book that moved the Earth, and the 300-year wait for direct proof. T1: Frombork, 24 May 1543 -- friends put into the hands of a stroke-paralysed cathedral canon, Nicolaus Copernicus, the first printed copy of the book he had held back for nearly thirty years; what that book did was demote the Earth to one planet among six, spinning daily and circling the Sun. T2: the puzzle it dissolved -- why Mars stops dead against the stars and loops BACKWARD for weeks: Earth on the faster inside track overtakes it, so the loop is a trick of our own motion (checkable in any sky-app). T3: Book I chapter 10's roll-call of periods -- Mercury 88 days, Venus ~9 months, Earth 1 year, Mars 2 years, Jupiter 12, Saturn 30 -- the planets nest in order of period outward; Ptolemy's arrangement never REQUIRED that order. T4: the unsigned preface 'Ad Lectorem', slipped in during printing by Lutheran theologian Andreas Osiander, told readers the hypotheses 'need not be true nor even probable'; Johannes Kepler later exposed Osiander as its author. T5: the corrected misconception -- the book was dedicated to Pope Paul III and drew no condemnation at all; Rome suspended it 'until corrected' only in 1616, seventy-three years later. T6: the honest caveat -- Copernicus kept perfect circles, still needed epicycles (about 34 circles in all), and his tables were no more accurate than Ptolemy's; he won on elegance, not precision. T7: what actually annoyed him was Ptolemy's EQUANT -- a fudge-point that let a planet sweep equal angles about a point that was not the centre of its own circle, breaking the ancient rule of uniform circular motion. T8: Georg Joachim Rheticus, the young Wittenberg mathematician who turned up uninvited in 1539 and became the only pupil Copernicus ever had, published the trailer (Narratio Prima, 1540) and carried the manuscript to printer Johannes Petreius in Nuremberg. T9: the killer objection -- if Earth swings across a vast orbit, nearby stars should shift against far ones over six months; nobody could see any such shift, and Copernicus's answer (the stars must be unimaginably far) struck Tycho Brahe as absurd. T10: James Bradley, hunting exactly that shift on Gamma Draconis from 1729, found a DIFFERENT one -- the aberration of starlight, about 20 arcseconds, precisely what you get if the observer is racing sideways through space: the first direct proof the Earth moves, 186 years after the book. T11: Friedrich Bessel finally caught true parallax in 1838 on 61 Cygni -- about a third of an arcsecond, a star some 11 light years off; Struve (Vega) and Henderson (Alpha Centauri) landed the same result within months. Copernicus's 'unimaginably far' was right. T12: the shape of the whole affair -- a claim published in 1543, its best objection unanswered until 1729, its direct confirmation in 1838. Science accepted it long before it could prove it, because it explained more.
source: Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' (1543 Nuremberg/Petreius; deathbed copy 24 May 1543; Osiander's Ad Lectorem and Kepler's exposure; retained epicycles, ~34 circles; retrograde from Earth overtaking; equant objection; Rheticus and Narratio Prima 1540; 1616 suspension). Wikipedia, 'Stellar parallax' (Tycho's objection; Bradley's aberration from 1729; Bessel/61 Cygni 1838; Struve and Henderson). Wikipedia, 'Nicolaus Copernicus' (death 24 May 1543; Commentariolus before 1514). Wikipedia, 'Copernican heliocentrism' (retrograde as parallactic displacement; no-parallax and star-size objections; no accuracy gain over Ptolemy).
framing_note: Flagship DISCOVERY ladder for the whole sub-strand, with an unusually strong honest-caveat spine. T1 puts Copernicus IN the stem as the scene anchor and keys the CLAIM as the answer -- never 'who wrote De revolutionibus?' (definition-shell, banned). Accuracy rail: do NOT say Copernicus made astronomy more accurate or simpler to compute -- he did not; his tables matched Ptolemy's and he kept epicycles. The honest version (elegance and a forced planetary order, not precision) is the interesting one. Second rail: the deathbed-copy account comes from Tiedemann Giese's letter to Rheticus -- present it as the recorded account, not as a bedside eyewitness scene, and do not embroider a moment of waking. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (Mars loops backward because WE overtake it -- go watch) and T10-T11 (the objection that stood for two centuries and the answer that finally came). Distractor mine: the graveyard of real rival cosmologies -- Ptolemy's equant and epicycles, Aristotle's crystalline spheres, the Tychonic compromise, Aristarchus of Samos's ancient heliocentrism -- plus real people (Rheticus, Osiander, Petreius, Bradley, Bessel) for the named-person rungs. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'because the Earth moves faster on an inner orbit' before asking why Mars appears to reverse.
history_overlap: history bank -- the Scientific Revolution / Renaissance printing as an era-episode, and the 1616 Index. Science keys the MODEL and its evidence (retrograde, planetary order, parallax), not the ecclesiastical or print-culture narrative.

name: Galileo's Starry Messenger
scope: Two months of looking through a homemade tube that broke the sky open. T1: 7 January 1610 -- three faint 'stars' in a neat row beside Jupiter; over the next nights they had MOVED, then a fourth appeared, and they were plainly circling Jupiter: the first moons ever seen around another world. T2: why that detonated -- everyone agreed everything in the heavens circles the Earth, and here were four objects visibly circling something that wasn't Earth. T3: Galileo named them the Medicean Stars for Cosimo II de' Medici and within months traded his Padua professorship for a Florentine court post at 1,000 florins with no teaching -- the discovery doubled as a job application, and he said so. T4: the corrected misconception -- Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are NOT Galileo's names; they come from his rival Simon Marius, on a suggestion from Kepler, and only became standard centuries later. T5: 30 November 1609 -- the Moon through the telescope is not a polished sphere but pitted and mountainous, and Galileo measured the mountains' HEIGHT from the length of their shadows near the sunrise line: geometry performed on another world. T6: the Milky Way, magnified, stopped being milk -- it dissolved into countless separate faint stars, so the band was never a cloud at all. T7: the corrected misconception on the instrument -- Galileo did not invent the telescope (Dutch spectacle-makers did, around 1608); he heard a description in 1609, worked out the optics and ground his own lenses to roughly 20x, later 30x. T8: Saturn defeated him -- in 1610 he saw two 'companions' or ears flanking the planet, and by 1612 they had VANISHED; he never solved it, and Christiaan Huygens explained the ring in 1655. T9: sunspots -- dark blotches crossing the Sun's face and returning on schedule, so the 'perfect, unchanging' Sun both rotates and blemishes; his priority quarrel with the Jesuit Christoph Scheiner was partly over whether the spots were ON the Sun or tiny satellites passing in front. T10: the book -- Sidereus Nuncius, a thin volume printed 13 March 1610, put the observations into print within weeks of making them, which is why the news outran the objections. T11: the practical payoff nobody expected -- Jupiter's moons eclipse on a strict schedule, so they are a clock every longitude on Earth can read at the same instant; Galileo pitched the method to Spain as a way to find longitude at sea.
source: Grokipedia, 'Galileo Galilei' (7 Jan 1610 three stars then a fourth; outer moon ~16.7-day period; Medicean Stars; Sidereus Nuncius published 13 March 1610; Moon sketches 30 Nov 1609 and shadow-based mountains; Milky Way resolved; ~20x rising to 30x; Medici post at 1,000 florins; Pisa-drop legend flagged as legendary). Grokipedia, 'Phases of Venus' (telescope ~20x; Venus disk 20-30 arcsec at elongation). Wikipedia, 'Galileo affair' (Simplicio and the Dialogue) for the downstream link only.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder; the most rung-dense topic in the sub-strand. Every stem must be scene-led -- 'Who discovered Jupiter's moons?' is banned; the T1 stem is the three dots that moved. Accuracy rail: Galileo did NOT invent the telescope and did NOT name the four moons -- both are near-universal misbeliefs and both are on-voice corrected-misconception rungs, so state the true attribution (Dutch spectacle-makers c.1608; Simon Marius, prompted by Kepler). Second rail: do not let the Leaning Tower drop leak into this ladder -- it is probably apocryphal and belongs to the physics motion ladder if used at all. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (he measured a mountain on the Moon from the length of its shadow -- and a kid with binoculars can see the same ragged sunrise line tonight) plus T1. Distractor mine: real rivals and real wrong models -- Simon Marius, Christoph Scheiner, Ptolemaic epicycles, Aristotle's incorruptible heavens, 'tiny satellites crossing the Sun' as the live alternative to sunspots. Lane border: Ole Roemer's 1676 use of Io's eclipse timings to measure the SPEED OF LIGHT belongs to the physics/light strand -- T11 keys the longitude-clock idea only, not light's finite speed.
history_overlap: history bank -- Medici patronage and Renaissance Florence as a court-politics episode. Science keys the OBSERVATIONS and the instrument; the patronage detail (T3) is kept only as the honest motive behind the naming.

name: The phases of Venus
scope: The observation that executed Ptolemy -- and did not do what everyone says it did. T1: seen through a telescope, Venus runs the same shape-cycle as the Moon -- thin crescent, half, gibbous, almost full -- and back again over 584 days. T2: invert the wonder -- Venus also swells and shrinks enormously, roughly 10 arcseconds across when nearly full and up to about 65 arcseconds as a thin crescent, six times wider; the crescent is the NEAR Venus, which is why a crescent Venus is so bright. T3: what that kills -- Ptolemy's arrangement pinned Venus to an epicycle that always sat between Earth and the Sun, so its lit face could never turn toward us; a Ptolemaic Venus can only ever be a crescent. A gibbous Venus is fatal to it. T4: the moment on paper -- Galileo's letter of 30 December 1610 to the Jesuit mathematician Christoph Clavius, reporting that Venus's disk, formerly circular, had 'acquired a semicircular shape', and predicting it would go crescent next: a prediction made in advance and then kept. T5: THE CORRECTION, and the point of the whole ladder -- the phases did not prove the Earth moves. Tycho Brahe's geo-heliocentric system (Earth fixed, Sun circling Earth, everything else circling the Sun) predicts exactly the same phases; Venus killed Ptolemy and left the Tychonic compromise standing for another century. T6: the precision detail -- Venus never quite reaches perfectly full from Earth, because at that point it is behind the Sun; the best it manages is a fat gibbous of about 99 per cent. T7: the mechanism you can check yourself -- Venus never wanders more than about 47 degrees from the Sun, which is why it is only ever a morning or evening 'star' and never overhead at midnight; that maximum elongation is the observation that pins Venus's orbit INSIDE Earth's.
source: Grokipedia, 'Phases of Venus' (Ptolemaic phase angle capped below 90 degrees so only crescents; Copernican and Tychonic both allow up to 180 degrees and gibbous/near-full; angular diameter ~10 arcsec at superior conjunction to ~65 arcsec at inferior; synodic period 583.92 days; max elongation 47 degrees; Galileo's 30 Dec 1610 letters to Clavius and Castelli with the 'semicircular shape' wording and the crescent prediction; never perfectly full, ~99 per cent maximum). Grokipedia, 'Galileo Galilei'.
framing_note: A short, hard, analytic ladder built around one CORRECTED MISCONCEPTION -- the single most-mistold fact in popular astronomy history. Accuracy rail (non-negotiable): the phases of Venus refute the PTOLEMAIC system, not geocentrism as such; Tycho's geo-heliocentric model predicts the identical phases, and the build must never write 'proved the Earth orbits the Sun'. Note that Grokipedia's own Galileo page phrases it loosely ('consistent only with heliocentrism') while its Phases of Venus page states the Tychonic equivalence correctly -- use the precise version. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the famous killer evidence killed something narrower than you were told) and T2 (six times wider). Distractor mine: real competing models only -- the Ptolemaic epicycle, the Tychonic system, the Copernican system, Heraclides' partial arrangement with Mercury and Venus circling the Sun; plus real rivals Clavius, Scheiner and Marius. Anti-restatement: the T3 stem must describe what Ptolemy's geometry FORCES (Venus always between us and the Sun) without naming 'only crescents' before the question asks it. If the anagram Galileo used to stake priority is wanted as an extra rung, verify the Latin and the recipient at build time before writing it.

name: The trial of 1633
scope: What actually happened, what the myths get wrong, and why the evidence outlived the verdict. T1: the 1632 book -- Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, staged as a conversation among three men, with the Earth-centred case given to a character named Simplicio. T2: the offence that turned a patron into a prosecutor -- Pope Urban VIII, previously Galileo's supporter, had asked for his own favourite argument to be included; Galileo put it in Simplicio's mouth, at the end, and Urban took it as mockery. T3: the 1616 backdrop -- Inquisition consultants had already declared the Sun-centred claim 'foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical'; Cardinal Bellarmine instructed Galileo to stop defending it, and De revolutionibus was suspended pending corrections. T4: the 1633 verdict -- not heresy but 'vehemently suspect of heresy'; Galileo read a prepared abjuration, and a formal sentence of imprisonment was commuted at once to house arrest, which he served in his own villa at Arcetri for the last nine years of his life. T5: the myth, told as a myth -- 'Eppur si muove' ('and yet it moves') appears in print for the first time in 1757, in a book by Giuseppe Baretti, 115 years after Galileo's death; no contemporary record has it. T6: the honest caveat that stings -- Galileo's own flagship PROOF that the Earth moves was his theory that the tides are the oceans sloshing under Earth's combined spin and orbit. It is wrong, and it was known to be shaky then; he had the right conclusion and a bad argument, and the first sound proof (Bradley's aberration) was a century away. T7: what he did under house arrest -- going blind, he wrote his best book, Discourses on Two New Sciences, and had the manuscript smuggled out to be printed in Leiden in 1638, beyond the Inquisition's reach; the physics in it fed straight into Newton. T8: the long postscript -- a papal commission opened in 1979 reported in 1992, when John Paul II acknowledged that the theologians of the day had erred.
source: Wikipedia, 'Galileo affair' (1616 consultants' 'foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical'; Bellarmine's injunction; De revolutionibus suspended pending correction; Urban VIII's argument given to Simplicio; 1633 'vehemently suspect of heresy'; house arrest at Arcetri; 'Eppur si muove' first attributed in print 1757 by Giuseppe Baretti; John Paul II's 1992 statement). Grokipedia, 'Galileo Galilei' (1633 trial for violating the 1616 injunction; abjuration; lifelong house arrest; works placed on the Index; Two New Sciences 1638).
framing_note: The one vision_mandated ladder in this sub-strand: it sits at the head of the bank's dissent arc (Galileo -> Semmelweis -> Wegener -> Marshall -> the Great Barrington authors -> Bhattacharya), so the moral audit must check it in BOTH directions. PRESENT, never preach: the record is damning without editorial. Accuracy rails, all load-bearing: (a) Galileo was never tortured and never held in a dungeon -- he was threatened with torture as a formal step and lodged in comfortable quarters, then his own villa; (b) do NOT conflate him with Giordano Bruno, who was burned in 1600 for a broad set of theological positions, not for Copernicanism; (c) 'Eppur si muove' must be told AS a legend with its 1757 first appearance; (d) T6's tide argument must be stated honestly -- this ladder is not hagiography, and the wrong-argument rung is what makes the censorship point land rather than preach it. Dinner-test payoff: T7 (banned, blind, under guard, he wrote the better book and smuggled it out). Distractor mine: real people and real positions -- Bellarmine, Urban VIII, Scheiner, the Jesuit astronomers who accepted the observations but kept the Tychonic model; and for T6, the real rival explanations of the tides (the Moon's pull, which Galileo rejected as astrology). Lane border: the Counter-Reformation and Church-state politics belong to HISTORY; philosophy owns the epistemology-of-authority seminar. Science keys the EVIDENCE and what happens when a test is forbidden.
history_overlap: history bank -- the Galileo trial as a Counter-Reformation / Church-authority episode, and the Index of Prohibited Books. Science must key the evidence and the suppression-of-a-test, not the ecclesiastical politics; if history already keys the 1633 verdict wording, science should lead on T5 (the myth), T6 (the wrong tide proof) and T7 (Two New Sciences smuggled to Leiden).

name: Tycho's data and Kepler's eight arcminutes
scope: The best measurements ever taken by naked eye, handed to the one man honest enough to let them kill his own beautiful theory. T1: Tycho Brahe worked entirely without a telescope -- none existed -- yet his star and planet positions were good to about one arcminute, roughly one-thirtieth the width of the full Moon and about five times better than anyone before him. T2: where -- Uraniborg, a castle-observatory begun in 1576 on the island of Hven on King Frederick II's money; when its towers proved too shaky in the wind he dug a second observatory, Stjerneborg (1584), with the instruments sunk underground. T3: 1572 -- a new star blazed in Cassiopeia, bright enough to see in daylight. Tycho measured it night after night and found NO daily parallax: it did not shift against the fixed stars, so it lay beyond the Moon. The unchangeable heavens had just changed. T4: 1577 -- a great comet; its parallax put it far beyond the Moon on a path that would have to smash straight through the crystalline spheres the planets supposedly rode on. The spheres were not there. T5: Tycho's own compromise -- Earth fixed at the centre, the Sun circling Earth, and every other planet circling the Sun; it fitted every observation available, including Venus's phases. T6: the corrected misconception about the famous nose -- part of Tycho's was cut off in a 1566 duel over a mathematics dispute, and the 2012 analysis of his exhumed remains found the prosthesis was BRASS, not the silver and gold of legend. T7: the second corrected misconception -- the 2010-2012 exhumation found far too little mercury in his remains to support the poisoning stories; Tycho was not murdered, and certainly not by Kepler. T8: 1600 -- Tycho hires a poor, short-sighted German mathematician, Johannes Kepler, and assigns him the worst planet: Mars. T9: Kepler's own beloved theory, from Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596), nested the five Platonic solids between the planetary spheres to explain their spacing. It was gorgeous. It was wrong. He kept testing it against Tycho's numbers anyway. T10: after years of grinding, Kepler built a circular model that matched Mars to within EIGHT ARCMINUTES -- about a quarter the width of the full Moon, better than any astronomer in history had managed. Any predecessor would have declared victory; but Tycho's data were good to one or two arcminutes, so eight could not be blamed on the observer. T11: Kepler's own sentence in Astronomia Nova (1609): 'Now, because they could not be disregarded, these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy.' He threw away the circle. T12: what replaced it -- an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; and the subtlety that makes the story, since Mars's ellipse is only about 0.4 per cent flatter than a circle and no eye could see the squash. What betrayed it was the SUN sitting about 9 per cent of the way off centre, so Mars runs measurably nearer and faster at one end -- the equal-areas law, which Kepler actually found BEFORE the ellipse. T13: 1619, Harmonices Mundi -- the third law: a planet's period squared is proportional to its distance cubed. Check it with a calculator: Jupiter sits 5.20 astronomical units out and 5.20 cubed is 140.6; Jupiter's year is 11.86 of ours and 11.86 squared is 140.7. One rule, every planet.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tycho Brahe' (Uraniborg 1576 on Hven under Frederick II; Stjerneborg 1584 underground; precision approaching one arcminute, ~5x Wilhelm of Hesse; 1572 Cassiopeia nova with no daily parallax; 1577 comet less parallax than the Moon, disproving solid spheres; 1566 duel and the 2012 brass-prosthesis finding; Tychonic geo-heliocentric system; death 24 Oct 1601 and the 2010-2012 conclusion of insufficient mercury). Wikipedia, 'Astronomia Nova' (published 1609; the eight-minute discrepancy and Kepler's quoted sentence; first two laws; area law found before the ellipse; ten years on Mars; Mars eccentricity ~0.09). Wikipedia, "Kepler's laws of planetary motion" (Harmonice Mundi 1619; T-squared proportional to a-cubed; Jupiter 11.86 yr at 5.20 AU; Mysterium Cosmographicum 1596 Platonic solids).
framing_note: The analytic backbone of the sub-strand -- a DISCOVERY ladder whose spine is intellectual honesty. Accuracy rail (this is the one that gets botched everywhere): Mars's eccentricity of about 0.09 does NOT mean the orbit is 9 per cent out of round. The semi-minor axis is only about 0.4 per cent shorter than the semi-major -- the shape is visually a circle -- while the SUN sits about 9 per cent of the semi-major axis off centre. Say it that way, and let the equal-areas speed variation, not a visibly squashed oval, be what exposes the ellipse. Second rail: Kepler found the second law before the first; do not narrate them in numbered order. Third rail: the mercury-murder story and the silver-nose story are both to be told as the debunked claims they are, with the exhumation as the test. Dinner-test payoff: T13 (a kid with a calculator confirms a law of the universe in twenty seconds -- do the same for Saturn, 9.54 cubed against 29.46 squared) and T11 (eight arcminutes he refused to ignore). Distractor mine: the real graveyard -- Ptolemy's equant, Copernicus's perfect circles, the Tychonic system, the crystalline spheres, and Kepler's own Platonic solids, which is the sharpest distractor available because he believed it himself. Anti-restatement: T10's stem gives the residual and Tycho's precision and asks what Kepler DID about it; it must never say 'the orbit is not a circle' first.

name: Herschel's accidental planet
scope: How a working musician doubled the solar system, and why the formula that seemed to predict it was not a law. T1: 13 March 1781, from the garden of 19 New King Street in Bath, a professional oboist and organist named William Herschel, sweeping the sky with a 6.2-inch reflector he had ground and built himself, found an object that was not a star -- and reported it as a comet. T2: how he knew it wasn't a star, and the bit a kid can copy tonight -- he kept increasing the magnification. Stars stayed stubborn points of light; this one swelled into a visible DISK. T3: it was not a comet either. Anders Johan Lexell computed the orbit and found it nearly circular and enormously far out; at roughly twice Saturn's distance from the Sun, Herschel had DOUBLED the size of the known solar system and added the first new planet in recorded history. T4: the naming fight -- Herschel called it Georgium Sidus after King George III, who gave him a royal pension for it; Johann Elert Bode proposed Uranus in 1782 on the grounds that the other planets carry mythological names, and Bode's choice had won by about 1850. T5: it had been seen and written down as a star at least twenty times -- John Flamsteed catalogued it in 1690 as '34 Tauri', and Pierre Charles Le Monnier logged it a dozen times between 1750 and 1769 without ever noticing it had moved. Evidence in plain sight, filtered out by what people expected to see. T6: the Titius-Bode 'law' -- an arithmetic recipe that reproduced the spacing of the known planets and put Uranus almost exactly where it turned out to be; its confidence sent astronomers hunting for a missing planet at 2.8 astronomical units, and Giuseppe Piazzi duly found Ceres there on 1 January 1801. T7: and then it broke. The rule puts the next planet near 39 astronomical units; Neptune sits at 30. A formula that fits the data you already have, with no mechanism underneath it, is a curve fit and not a law of nature -- and this one had already fooled the best astronomers of two generations.
source: Wikipedia, 'Uranus' (Herschel 13 March 1781 from 19 New King Street, Bath; homemade 6.2-inch reflector; reported as a comet 26 April 1781; Lexell computed the orbit; Bode's near-circular-orbit argument; Georgium Sidus vs Bode's 'Uranus' 1782, universal by 1850; Flamsteed's 1690 '34 Tauri' and Le Monnier's dozen sightings 1750-1769; roughly twice Saturn's distance). Grokipedia, 'IAU definition of planet' (Ceres found by Piazzi 1 January 1801 at the Titius-Bode gap, hailed as the eighth planet, reclassified after Pallas and others by 1850). Wikipedia, 'Discovery of Neptune' (Le Verrier and Adams both used Bode's law and overshot to ~36 AU).
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder with a genuine method payload in the last two rungs. T1 keys the ACT and the honest error (he called it a comet), not a date -- 'in what year was Uranus discovered' is banned. Dinner-test payoff: T2 -- crank up the magnification and a star stays a point while a planet becomes a disk; any kid with binoculars on Jupiter versus a bright star can run the same test in one evening, which is exactly the test-it-yourself soul. Accuracy rail: do not call Herschel an amateur in a dismissive sense or a professional astronomer in 1781 -- he earned his living from music and had built better telescopes than the Royal Observatory's; and do not say Bode's rule 'predicted' Uranus in advance, since Uranus was found first and then found to fit. Distractor mine: real objects and real people -- a comet, a distant star, Ceres, Flamsteed, Le Monnier, Lexell, Bode, Piazzi. T7 sets up the Vulcan and Neptune ladders: Bode's rule is the shared wrong assumption that made Le Verrier's Neptune orbit badly wrong, so cross-key it rather than repeating it there.

name: Neptune found on paper
scope: A planet located by arithmetic before any eye had knowingly seen it. T1: 23 September 1846 -- Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory opens a letter from Paris, points the telescope where the letter says, and with his student Heinrich d'Arrest finds a new planet the SAME NIGHT, less than an hour into the search and under one degree from the predicted spot. T2: the letter's author, Urbain Le Verrier, had not been looking through a telescope at all; he had computed the planet's place from the misbehaviour of a different one. T3: the misbehaviour -- Alexis Bouvard's 1821 tables for Uranus kept failing: the planet ran ahead of schedule, then fell behind it, and Bouvard himself suggested an unseen body was pulling on it. T4: what makes the calculation so hard -- it is the problem run backwards. Normally you know the masses and predict the motion; Le Verrier had the motion and had to solve for an unknown mass at an unknown distance, with Newton's law assumed to be exactly true. T5: the detail that settled it on the night -- d'Arrest fetched a brand-new star chart, and the object they were looking at was not on it. T6: the priority fight -- John Couch Adams had reached a similar answer in England in 1845, but communicated it vaguely to Astronomer Royal George Airy; James Challis at Cambridge began searching only in July 1846, had no up-to-date chart, and actually RECORDED Neptune on 8 and 12 August without recognising it. T7: the honest caveat -- Le Verrier's predicted ORBIT was badly wrong. Leaning on Bode's rule he placed the planet near 36 astronomical units; Neptune is at 30. His numbers happened to be close over the short arc of sky that mattered in 1846, so real luck rode along with the mathematics. T8: the earlier near-miss -- Galileo's notebooks record the object on 28 December 1612 and 27 January 1613, sitting near Jupiter; he even noted it appeared to have shifted, then filed it as a fixed star. Two hundred and thirty-three years early. T9: why this discovery carried such weight -- Newton's law of gravity had made a specific, unhedged, falsifiable prediction about an object nobody had ever seen, and collected on it within an hour. Being able to lose is what makes a prediction worth anything. T10: Neptune's year is about 165 Earth years, so it finished its first complete orbit since discovery in 2011 -- one lap of the planet the mathematics found before the eye did.
source: Wikipedia, 'Discovery of Neptune' (Bouvard's 1821 tables and his unseen-body hypothesis; Le Verrier's results posted 31 August 1846, received by Galle 23 September and observed that night; found in under an hour and less than one degree from the prediction; d'Arrest's up-to-date chart; Adams's 1845 calculation, Airy and Challis's delay, Challis's unrecognised 8 and 12 August observations; both Adams and Le Verrier overestimated the distance using Bode's law, Le Verrier at ~36 AU against the true 30 AU, yet accurate over the relevant arc; Galileo's 28 December 1612 and 27 January 1613 observations mistaken for a fixed star).
framing_note: Flagship PREDICTION ladder; deliberately paired with the Vulcan ladder, which is the same method failing -- cross-key them so no fact repeats across the two. T1 keys the RESULT and the speed (same night, under one degree), with Galle and d'Arrest named in the stem; never 'who discovered Neptune?'. Accuracy rail: resist the tidy legend that Le Verrier's mathematics was flawless -- his orbit was substantially wrong (36 AU vs 30) and the ladder must carry T7 honestly, because the bank's whole point is that a real success is more interesting than a clean one. Second rail: the Adams-versus-Le Verrier credit story should be told as a communication failure and a nationalist quarrel, not as an English hero robbed. Dinner-test payoff: T1 and T8 (Galileo had it in his notebook 233 years early, noticed it move, and let it go). Distractor mine: real adjacent science and real people -- Bode's law, a comet, an error in the tables, a moon of Uranus, and Bouvard, Adams, Airy, Challis, Arago, d'Arrest as named-person options. Anti-restatement: T4's stem must set up the difficulty without naming 'inverse problem' as a term the answer then supplies -- teach the idea in plain words first.

name: Vulcan, the planet that wasn't
scope: The same method, the same man, the opposite result -- and why that is the most useful failure in astronomy. T1: fresh from Neptune, Urbain Le Verrier turned the trick on Mercury, whose closest point to the Sun creeps around by 43 arcseconds per century more than Newton's gravity can account for once every known planet's pull is subtracted. His conclusion: another unseen planet, this one closer in. He called it Vulcan. T2: a country doctor named Edmond Lescarbault wrote to say he had SEEN it -- a small black dot crossing the Sun's face on 26 March 1859. Le Verrier travelled to the village, interrogated him, believed him, announced Vulcan to the Academy on 2 January 1860, and had Lescarbault decorated with the Legion d'honneur. T3: the sightings kept arriving and kept not repeating. At the total solar eclipse of 29 July 1878, two respected American astronomers -- James Craig Watson in Wyoming and Lewis Swift near Denver -- each reported a reddish object near the Sun, and their positions did not agree with each other. T4: why nobody could simply go and check -- a planet inside Mercury's orbit is only visible in transit across the Sun or during the couple of minutes of a total eclipse. It is the perfect hiding place for a thing that is not there. T5: the resolution came in November 1915 from a direction nobody was looking -- Einstein's general relativity, in which mass curves spacetime so that an orbit close to a very massive body does not quite close on itself; the extra drift it predicts for Mercury came out at 43 arcseconds per century, with nothing adjustable to make it fit. Not a missing planet. A missing THEORY. T6: the pairing that teaches the lesson -- with Uranus, blaming the anomaly on unseen matter was right and produced Neptune; with Mercury, the identical move produced nothing. The method is sound; what it cannot tell you in advance is which kind of failure you are staring at. T7: the live version -- astronomers today infer dark matter from galaxies rotating far too fast for their visible mass, which is exactly Le Verrier's move again. Whether it is Neptune (real unseen matter) or Vulcan (a law of gravity that needs amending, as modified-gravity theorists argue) is not known. Say so. T8: and the human postscript -- Lescarbault was not a fraud, Watson and Swift were not cranks; they were competent people who saw something and reported it honestly. Careful observers produce wrong results, which is the whole reason a result has to repeat before anyone believes it.
source: Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)' (43 arcseconds per century unexplained; Lescarbault's claimed transit of 26 March 1859; Le Verrier's announcement 2 January 1860 and the Legion d'honneur; the 29 July 1878 eclipse claims by James Craig Watson in Wyoming and Lewis Swift near Denver, both describing a reddish object; Einstein's 1915 general relativity removing the need for the planet by accounting for exactly 43 arcseconds per century via spacetime curvature). Wikipedia, 'Discovery of Neptune' (for the paired-method contrast).
framing_note: A MYSTERY-plus-REVERSAL ladder, and the sharpest method lesson in the sub-strand; deliberately paired with the Neptune ladder. Accuracy rail: Le Verrier presented the Mercury anomaly in 1859 and announced the supposed confirmation on 2 January 1860 -- keep the two dates distinct. Also do NOT put an undocumented Einstein quotation in a stem: the widely repeated 'heart palpitations' reaction traces to second-hand recollection and could not be verified in the sources consulted here, so either omit it or verify it against Pais or the Einstein Papers before it goes anywhere near a record. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the anomaly was not a hidden planet but a hole in Newton's gravity) and T7 (the identical argument is running right now over dark matter, and nobody yet knows the answer). Distractor mine: the real live alternatives, used honestly -- an unseen intra-Mercurial planet, a ring of dust or asteroids inside Mercury's orbit, a slightly oblate Sun, a small modification to the inverse-square law (modified gravity is a real minority research programme, never a joke option), and mismeasurement of Mercury itself. On T7 the bank must not let a distractor secretly be the truth: dark matter is unresolved and the record must say so. Lane border: the 1919 eclipse test of light-bending, gravitational time dilation and the rest of general relativity belong to the physics/relativity ladder -- key ONLY Mercury's 43 arcseconds here.

name: Halley's comet keeps its appointment
scope: A dead man's prediction, kept to within a month, seventy-six years out. T1: in 1705 Edmond Halley noticed that the comets recorded in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had nearly identical orbits, and argued they were ONE comet coming back; then he did the thing that made it science and put a date on the next return -- around 1758, when he would be long dead. T2: the refinement -- Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute spent months computing how the pull of Jupiter and Saturn would DELAY the comet, found the delay came to about 618 days, and named 13 April 1759 for perihelion while openly stating a month of uncertainty. It arrived on 13 March 1759: a month early, and inside their own stated error bars. T3: the first person to see it return was not an astronomer at all -- Johann Georg Palitzsch, a German farmer, picked it up on Christmas night, 25 December 1758. T4: Halley had died in 1742, sixteen years before the comet came back; the comet was named for him afterwards, by other people. T5: what the return actually settled -- comets are not omens, not signs, and not fires in the upper air; they are ordinary members of the solar system on long stretched orbits, obeying exactly the same law as the planets. T6: the corrected misconception about what a comet IS -- when the Giotto probe flew past the nucleus in 1986 it photographed a peanut-shaped lump about 15 by 8 by 8 kilometres that reflects only about 4 per cent of the light falling on it, darker than coal. The bright thing in the sky is gas and dust boiled off that dark lump by sunlight. T7: 19 May 1910 -- Earth passed through the comet's tail. Spectroscopes had found the poison cyanogen in the tail, newspapers ran with it and hucksters sold anti-comet pills; nothing whatever happened, because a comet's tail is emptier than most laboratory vacuums. T8: the standing invitation -- it comes back in 2061. Work out how old you will be. Halley's real achievement was handing everyone after him an appointment they could check.
source: Wikipedia, "Halley's Comet" (1705 Synopsis linking the 1531, 1607 and 1682 apparitions and predicting a 1758 return; Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute computing a ~618-day Jupiter-Saturn delay and predicting 13 April 1759 against an actual perihelion of 13 March 1759; Johann Georg Palitzsch's first sighting on 25 December 1758; Halley's death in 1742; Giotto's 1986 nucleus of about 15 x 8 x 8 km with an albedo of 0.04, 'about what one would expect for coal'; Earth's passage through the tail on 19 May 1910, the cyanogen scare and the anti-comet pills; next return around 2061).
framing_note: A PREDICTION ladder whose payoff is an invitation rather than a fact. Dinner-test payoff: T8 -- the kid does the subtraction and discovers they have a date with a comet, which is the purest form of this bank's test-it-yourself soul. Accuracy rail: give Clairaut's team's prediction WITH its stated uncertainty; a bare '13 April predicted, 13 March actual' reads as a miss, whereas the honest version -- a month early, inside a month of declared error -- is the more impressive and the more scientific fact, and it teaches error bars without a definition. Second rail: Nicole-Reine Lepaute did a large share of that computation and should be named as a computer alongside Clairaut and Lalande, on the record, without any DEI reframing. Distractor mine: the real historical wrong answers -- omens and portents, Aristotle's burning exhalations in the upper atmosphere, a passing star, a moon torn loose -- plus the real people (Newton, Clairaut, Lepaute, Palitzsch, Messier). Lane borders: the PHYSICS gravity ladder owns Newton's Principia and the inverse-square law itself; this ladder keys the prediction-and-return only. HISTORY owns the 1066 apparition on the Bayeux Tapestry -- do not key it here.
history_overlap: history bank -- the 1066 apparition on the Bayeux Tapestry and the Norman Conquest. Do not key 1066 in this ladder. Also flag the physics/gravity strand, which owns Newton's law itself.

name: How far is the Sun? The transits of Venus
scope: A perfect map with no scale on it, and the century-long global campaign to measure one distance. T1: Kepler's laws delivered a flawless map of the solar system in RELATIVE units -- Venus at 0.72, Mars at 1.52, Jupiter at 5.20 -- but nothing anywhere told you how many miles those units were. Measure one real distance and every other one follows. T2: Edmond Halley's 1716 paper named the method -- watch Venus cross the Sun's face from two widely separated places on Earth, and because each observer sees it cross a slightly different chord, the crossings take slightly different times; that difference yields the parallax, and the parallax yields the distance. Halley knew the next transits fell in 1761 and 1769 and that he would be dead for both. He wrote instructions for people who had not been born. T3: the first human being ever to watch one -- Jeremiah Horrocks, aged twenty, at Much Hoole in Lancashire on 24 November 1639 (Julian calendar). He had recomputed Kepler's tables himself and realised they had missed a transit entirely; he projected the Sun's image through a telescope onto a sheet of paper and watched the black dot arrive. His figure for the Sun's distance came out near 96 million kilometres -- two-thirds of the truth, and far better than anything before it. T4: 1761 and 1769 became the first global scientific campaign in history -- dozens of expeditions to Siberia, Newfoundland, Madagascar, the Cape of Good Hope and Tahiti, financed by rival governments that kept cooperating through a war. T5: for 1769 the Royal Society sent James Cook and the Endeavour to Tahiti, to a headland still called Point Venus. T6: the disaster -- Guillaume Le Gentil sailed for India for the 1761 transit, was still at sea (where no measurement is possible) when it happened, decided to WAIT eight years for the next one, and was clouded out on the morning of it. He got home after eleven years to find himself declared dead, his estate divided among his relatives and his seat at the Academy filled. T7: what defeated all of them -- the 'black drop': as Venus's disk meets the Sun's edge it seems to stretch a dark ligament, so the exact instant of contact cannot be timed. The method needed a precision that the eye and the atmosphere simply would not give. T8: the best nineteenth-century answer, from Encke's 1824 reanalysis of both transits, was about 153.3 million kilometres; the true value is 149.6 million -- an error of two and a half per cent, wrung out of ships, clouds and black drops. T9: the real answer arrived by a completely different route -- in the early 1960s radar teams bounced radio pulses off Venus and timed the echo, fixing the astronomical unit to within metres. The transits' value lay in the attempt, and in what the attempt built. T10: the sting in the invitation -- transits come in pairs eight years apart and then nothing for over a century. The last pair was 2004 and 2012. The next is December 2117. Nobody reading this will see one.
source: Wikipedia, 'Transit of Venus' (Halley's 1716 proposal of the parallax method; Jeremiah Horrocks's first recorded observation from Much Hoole using telescope projection onto paper, with an Earth-Sun estimate of about 95.6 million km; the 1761 and 1769 international expeditions to Siberia, Newfoundland, Madagascar, Tahiti and the Cape; Cook's observation from Point Venus, Tahiti in 1769; Le Gentil's eight-year misfortune and being declared dead; the black-drop effect degrading timing; the 8-year pair spacing with 105.5 or 121.5-year gaps; the next pair in December 2117 and 2125). Wikipedia, "Kepler's laws of planetary motion" (relative distances only, no absolute scale).
framing_note: Keystone SCALE ladder -- the sub-strand's answer to 'how do we know how big any of this is?'. Accuracy rails: (a) Horrocks's date is 24 November 1639 on the Julian calendar England then used, equal to 4 December Gregorian -- give one and say which, never both unlabelled; (b) Encke's 153.3 million km figure is his 1824 reanalysis, not a 1769 result -- do not compress the timeline; (c) verify Le Gentil's specific losses at build time before writing the estate and Academy details into a stem, and do not embellish the wife-remarried version, which varies between retellings. Dinner-test payoff: T10 (a scientific event a person can be too early AND too late for) and T6 (Le Gentil, eleven years, zero data, declared dead). Distractor mine: the real rival methods for measuring the solar system -- Cassini and Richer's 1672 Mars parallax from Paris and Cayenne, Aristarchus's half-moon geometry, lunar eclipse shadow timing, Eratosthenes' shadow (which sizes the Earth, not the Sun's distance) -- plus the real people (Halley, Horrocks, Cook, Le Gentil, Encke, Delisle). Anti-restatement: T2's stem describes two observers on far-apart parts of the Earth seeing the same crossing; it must not use the word parallax before the answer does.
history_overlap: history bank -- Cook's Pacific voyages and the Endeavour, including the sealed Admiralty orders to search for the southern continent; geography bank -- Tahiti as a place. Science must key the MEASUREMENT (why two distant observers give the Sun's distance) and use Cook only as the anchor, never touring the voyage.

name: Eclipses predicted to the minute
scope: How anyone knew, centuries in advance, exactly where on Earth the shadow would fall. T1: total solar eclipses are not rare -- one happens somewhere on Earth roughly every eighteen months -- but the shadow's track is usually under two hundred kilometres wide, so any one town waits centuries. The rarity is about WHERE, not whether. T2: the pattern the Babylonians extracted from centuries of records: eclipses repeat on a cycle of 223 lunar months -- 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours, later called the saros. Know one eclipse and you know one 18 years later. T3: the catch is those 8 hours. An extra third of a day means the Earth has spun a further 120 degrees, so the next eclipse of the series lands about a third of the way around the world; stack three saroses -- 54 years, the exeligmos -- and the shadow comes back near your own longitude. T4: the object that proves how far this went -- the Antikythera mechanism, a bronze geared device from the second century BC hauled off a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera in 1901. Its back carries a spiral saros dial with glyphs in 51 of its 223 month-cells naming 38 lunar and 27 solar eclipses, complete with the hour, plus a separate exeligmos dial for adding the 8-hour corrections. Nothing of comparable complexity reappears for about 1,500 years. T5: why eclipses are not monthly -- the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's, so at most new moons the Moon passes above or below the Sun; only when a new moon falls near one of the two crossing points can a shadow reach the ground. T6: the coincidence nobody can explain away -- the Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun and happens to sit about 400 times closer, so the two look almost exactly the same size from here; that is why totality is a knife-edge, and why the Moon sometimes leaves a ring of Sun uncovered when it is at the far end of its slightly egg-shaped orbit. T7: and it is temporary. Laser pulses fired at the mirror arrays Apollo 11, 14 and 15 left on the Moon -- still in daily use, the distance now known to millimetres -- show the Moon drifting away about 3.8 centimetres a year, so total eclipses have an expiry date. Meanwhile the published tables give contact times to the second: a kid with the table, a clock and a clear sky can check the prediction against the universe personally.
source: Wikipedia, 'Saros (astronomy)' (6,585.32 days = 18 years 11 days 8 hours = 223 synodic months; the one-third-day remainder shifting the next eclipse ~120 degrees west; the exeligmos triple saros of 19,755.96 days restoring local time; Chaldean/neo-Babylonian origin; the saros alone being insufficient to fix the exact path). Wikipedia, 'Antikythera mechanism' (second century BC; recovered 1901 from the Antikythera wreck; 223-month saros spiral with glyphs in 51 cells naming 38 lunar and 27 solar eclipses with day and hour; exeligmos dial; at least 30 gears; nothing comparable for ~1,500 years). Wikipedia, 'Lunar Laser Ranging experiment' (retroreflector arrays left by Apollo 11, 14 and 15; recession of 3.8 cm/year; millimetre precision; still in use).
framing_note: A MECHANISM ladder built to end in an invitation. Dinner-test payoff: T7 -- go find the published time for your own location and hold a clock to the sky; and T4, a 2,000-year-old bronze computer that named eclipses by the hour. Accuracy rails: (a) the saros predicts RECURRENCE, not the precise track of totality -- do not let a rung claim the Babylonians could say which country would go dark; (b) if the Thales 585 BC prediction is used at all it must be told AS the legend it is, since the sources do not support the claim that the method available to him could have delivered it; (c) do not attach a specific figure to when total eclipses will cease -- published estimates vary by hundreds of millions of years -- say 'eventually' unless a figure is verified at build time. Distractor mine: real cycles and real rival ideas -- the 19-year Metonic cycle (real, different purpose), the 8-year Venus cycle, the draconic month, and the historically genuine wrong explanations (a dragon or beast devouring the Sun, an omen of a king's death). Lane borders: geography owns eclipse-path PLACES; the ANIMAL bank owns animal behaviour during totality; the Apollo landings as an exploration and evidence story belong to the space-exploration sub-strand -- T7 keys the RECESSION measurement only.
history_overlap: history bank -- the Thales/Halys battle legend and Babylonian astronomy as an ancient-civilisation episode. Science keys the CYCLE and its mechanism; if the legend is used, key it only as a debunked attribution.

name: Pluto's demotion
scope: Not a scandal -- a category honestly applied, and the world that turned out to be alive. T1: 18 February 1930 -- Clyde Tombaugh, a 24-year-old Kansas farm boy hired at Lowell Observatory to photograph the same patch of sky twice, flicked between two plates in a blink comparator and caught the single dot that had shifted. T2: the name came from an 11-year-old -- Venetia Burney of Oxford suggested 'Pluto' over breakfast; her grandfather passed it to an astronomer friend and the observatory adopted it. T3: the irony under the whole story -- Tombaugh was hunting 'Planet X', predicted by Percival Lowell from wobbles in Uranus's orbit, and Pluto turned up about six degrees from one of Lowell's positions. But Pluto is roughly one five-hundredth of Earth's mass, far too feeble to tug Uranus at all, and when Voyager 2 measured Neptune's mass slightly lower in 1989 the wobbles themselves evaporated. A right answer for a wrong reason, and it took sixty years to say so out loud. T4: the precedent nobody remembered -- Ceres, found by Giuseppe Piazzi on 1 January 1801, was called the eighth planet for decades; then Pallas appeared, then dozens more in the same belt, and by the 1850s the lot of them had been reclassified as asteroids. Pluto's story had already happened once. T5: what forced the question again -- Mike Brown, Chad Trujillo and David Rabinowitz found Eris out beyond Pluto in 2005 and first measured it as BIGGER. Either the solar system had a tenth planet and probably a fiftieth, or the word 'planet' needed an actual definition. T6: the definition adopted in Prague on 24 August 2006 -- a planet orbits the Sun, is round under its own gravity, and has CLEARED its orbital neighbourhood. Pluto passes the first two and fails the third, sharing the Kuiper belt with thousands of bodies. T7: the road not taken -- the committee's earlier draft used only 'orbits the Sun' plus 'round', which would have kept Pluto and ADDED Ceres, Charon and Eris, giving a twelve-planet solar system; astronomers including Alan Stern still argue that the geophysical definition is the better one. This is a live scientific disagreement, not a closed verdict. T8: and the twist -- when New Horizons flew past on 14 July 2015 the supposed dead ice ball had water-ice mountains kilometres high and a vast plain of nitrogen ice, Sputnik Planitia, whose surface is churning in convection cells and carries essentially no impact craters, meaning it is being resurfaced now. What keeps a world that small and that cold geologically alive is not yet known.
source: Wikipedia, 'Pluto' (Tombaugh's discovery 18 February 1930 with a blink comparator; Venetia Burney, aged 11, of Oxford; the 3:2 resonance with Neptune and the ~8 AU separation despite Pluto being inside Neptune's orbit 1979-1999; New Horizons on 14 July 2015, Sputnik Planitia's convecting nitrogen-ice cells, near-absence of craters, water-ice mountains such as Tenzing Montes; diameter 2,376.6 km). Wikipedia, 'Planet X' (Lowell's prediction from Uranian residuals; Pluto found about six degrees from a predicted position; Charon's 1978 discovery fixing Pluto's mass near 1/500 Earth's, far too small; Voyager 2's revised Neptune mass eliminating the residuals; the verdict that the prediction was accidental). Grokipedia, 'IAU definition of planet' (Resolution B5 adopted 24 August 2006 in Prague, the three criteria, the dwarf-planet category; Ceres found 1 January 1801 by Piazzi, hailed as the eighth planet, reclassified after Pallas by 1850; Eris found 2005 by Brown, Trujillo and Rabinowitz and first estimated larger than Pluto; the Gingerich committee's geophysical draft that would have admitted Ceres, Charon and Eris; Alan Stern's objections).
framing_note: A ladder about how science updates its own CATEGORIES, and the sub-strand's third outcome of the prediction method (Neptune succeeded, Vulcan failed, Pluto was a coincidence dressed as a success) -- cross-key those three so no fact repeats. Accuracy rails: (a) Eris was first estimated LARGER than Pluto and is now known to be very slightly smaller in diameter while about 27 per cent more massive -- state whichever is used precisely, never a bare 'bigger'; (b) the Voyager 2 Neptune-mass revision is the fact that killed Planet X, and it must not be softened into 'Lowell was basically right'; (c) Pluto was never in danger of hitting Neptune -- the 3:2 resonance and the 17-degree tilt keep them roughly 8 AU apart at closest, and this makes a good alternate rung if one is needed; (d) verify the specific height of Tenzing Montes at build time before putting a number in a stem. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (an 11-year-old named a planet at breakfast) and T8 (the dead ice ball has no craters, so something is still resurfacing it, and nobody knows what). Frame T6 as an honest application of a rule rather than a demotion or an insult, and let T7 keep the disagreement live -- the bank does not pretend a contested classification is settled. Distractor mine: real bodies and real criteria -- Ceres, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Charon, Sedna, Quaoar, and the criteria Pluto actually passes (round, orbits the Sun, has moons) as near-miss options. On T8 no distractor may secretly be the true explanation of Pluto's activity; the record must say plainly that it is unresolved.
